speaker_role: current admissions officer(s) (unnamed, multiple speakers described as admissions/university staff giving direct-to-camera advice)
key_insights: Admissions readers use recommendation letters to picture the student as a 'presence' in a classroom, since a university is fundamentally made up of many classrooms

Teachers who give specific classroom anecdotes (e.g., whether a student is one who always raises their hand or one who rarely speaks but changes the conversation when they do) are seen as most helpful

Recommends students sit down with the recommending teacher and provide four or five bullet points reminding them of specific work/moments in class (e.g., a particular paper or group project) so the letter can be personalized rather than generic
Identifies the 'template recommendation' - a form letter with generic phrases like 'good student, works hard' where only names/activities are swapped - as the biggest problem admissions officers see
Advises students to help teachers avoid template letters by supplying specific, concrete examples and reminders of who they were in that classroom

Describes a concept of 'separating': a strong letter explicitly distinguishes the student from the broader group (e.g., calling them 'a top student in 10 years') rather than just calling them a 'good student'
notable_or_distinctive: The 'separating' concept - whether a letter explicitly marks a student as standing out from peers versus just being generically good - is a specific, actionable evaluative lens not commonly named in generic recommendation-letter advice.
reliability_notes: Speakers are not named or credentialed on screen within the transcript itself (identified only as admissions perspective via context/channel), so their specific institutional authority cannot be verified from the transcript alone; content is short and general but consistent with widely-cited admissions guidance.
